Analytical Integration: The notebook successfully bridges complex spatial accessibility modeling with interactive web cartography, translating raw travel-time metrics into a clear, multi-category Car Dependency Index.

Actionable Spatial Insights: By overlaying CDI classifications with IRSD socioeconomic data and clipped OSM road infrastructure, the workflow highlights critical equity hotspots across Burnie that require targeted transport policy interventions.

Reproducible Workflow: Built using open-source geospatial tools (geopandas, folium, branca), the pipeline provides a scalable, publication-ready prototype that can be readily adapted to evaluate car dependency in other regional Australian centres.

Visual Hierarchy & Contrast: The dark charcoal basemap (#1B1C24) combined with muted road vectors (#AEB6B8) ensures that the CDI choropleth polygons remain the primary visual focus, providing high contrast for quick spatial pattern recognition.

Information Layering & Density: Separating quick-reference hover tooltips (CDI category and accessibility metrics) from comprehensive click popups (IRSD scores, population, and modal gravity outputs) prevents visual clutter while retaining full data transparency.

Cartographic Trade-offs: Filtering and clipping OpenStreetMap road network vectors directly to the unified Burnie SA1 boundary reduces feature counts from 5,112 to 4,059, optimizing web rendering performance without sacrificing structural roadway context.

Model Limitations: The static 30-minute gravity catchment model assumes uniform departure times and fixed transit schedules, which may underestimate spatial reliance during off-peak hours or weekend service reductions across peripheral SA1s.

This spatial analysis project evaluates Car Dependency and Essential-Service Accessibility in Burnie, Tasmania. Regional coastal hubs often experience high private vehicle reliance due to dispersed residential layouts and complex topography.

Note

This study integrates cadastral parcels of Burnie sourced from the LIST, which were essential for defining study area boundaries through precise spatial clipping. To evaluate commuting patterns, ABS census data was extracted to examine prevailing transport modes, specifically distinguishing between private vehicle usage and public bus transit. Furthermore, Points of Interest (POIs) extracted from the LIST were mapped to identify essential amenities, including healthcare facilities, retail shops, and community hubs.

Educational accessibility was explicitly modeled using schools data from the LIST to assess travel time proximity for families and children. To contextualize spatial equity, the Socio-Economic Indexes for Areas (SEIFA) were imported from the ABS, providing critical indicators of relative socio-economic advantage and disadvantage across regions. Finally, public transport infrastructure was incorporated by extracting Metro bus stop locations, enabling comparative travel-time calculations between private automobile trips and public transit services.



Overview of the Burnie spatial study area and loaded shapefile layers within the workspace.

Library Setup & Path Configuration: Loaded geospatial and mapping libraries including geopandas, pandas, folium, and branca, and established project directory paths.

Data Ingestion:Loaded the final six-category CDI and equity layer (burnie_car_dependency_equity_6categories.gpkg) containing 56 SA1 features reprojected to EPSG:4326.

Loaded OpenStreetMap road features for Burnie and clipped them to the unified Burnie SA1 boundary outline (reducing features from 5,112 to 4,059).

Data Preparation: Formatted display attributes for population, IRSD scores, car/PT accessibility metrics, CDI values, and equity priority flags.

Map Styling & Construction:Built a custom dark-themed map (#1B1C24) using Folium.

Added the road network layer with stylized weights and opacities based on road class (fclass).Implemented a 5-class color scale (#2166AC to #D73027) representing lower to higher car advantage.Configured interactive hover tooltips and click popups displaying demographic and accessibility metrics.Injected custom HTML/CSS for a floating map title and a compact CDI legend.

Mathematical Formulation
The Car Dependency Index (CDI) is a model that evaluates how easily populations at origin i can reach essential opportunities j (such as employment, education, and healthcare) across different transportCDI_i = \frac{O_{i,\text{Car}} - O_{i,\text{PT}}}{O_{i,\text{Car}} + O_{i,\text{PT}}}

Where:

A_i represents the cumulative accessibility score for origin zone i.

O_j is the magnitude of opportunities available at destination j.

t_{ij} is the network travel time between origin i and destination j.

\beta is the distance-decay parameter reflecting traveler sensitivity to travel time.

By comparing accessibility via private motor vehicles (A_i^{car}) against public transit (A_i^{pt}), the index derives a comparative ratio, quantifying the systemic advantage and reliance on private automobiles across regional mesh blocks.

Output Artifact: Executing the notebook generates the publication-ready Burnie CDI 30-Min Interactive Map Display, rendering 56 SA1 polygon features and 4,059 clipped OpenStreetMap road segments over a custom dark base (#1B1C24).

Spatial Categorization & Model Advantage:

Categories 1 & 2 (Public Transit Advantage / Parity): Concentrated in central Burnie and inner suburbs, where high stop density yields competitive public transit travel times (A_i^{\text{pt}} \approx A_i^{\text{car}}).

Categories 3 & 4 (Moderate to High Dependency): Covers middle-ring residential zones (e.g., Shorewell Park, Acton) where service frequencies drop and transfer delays expand the A_i^{\text{car}} / A_i^{\text{pt}} gap.

Categories 5 & 6 (Severe & Extreme Disadvantage): Dominates peri-urban and steep peripheral SA1s (e.g., Havenview, Ridgley fringe), where transit options fail to provide functional access within 30 minutes.

Equity & Disadvantage Overlap: Cross-tabulating the 6 CDI categories with IRSD scores identifies specific high-priority SA1s where low socio-economic status intersects with high automotive reliance.
